notes.h: The idea of human alteration (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A biome (a large natural community of plants and animals, shaped by climate) has a natural state. People have changed almost every one, and the exam asks how.
points: Natural (climax) vegetation is what would grow if the land were left undisturbed. Very little of the earth's land remains untouched, so most biomes now show some human influence.
Humans alter biomes by removing, replacing or degrading vegetation, changing soils and water, introducing or removing species, and polluting.
The effects reach every part of the system, because the parts are linked: climate, soil, plants, animals and people all change together.
notes.tip: Exams ask how human activity alters biomes. Use named examples and give specific impacts on vegetation, animals, soils and climate.

notes.h: Early settlement: Ireland's post-glacial forest (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Before people changed it, Ireland's natural vegetation was forest. The forest spread as the ice retreated.
points: After the last glaciation (the last ice age) ended about 10,000 years ago, Ireland was colonised first by birch and hazel, then by pine, oak, elm and ash.
By about 6,000 years ago forest covered almost all of the island. This was the temperate deciduous forest biome (broadleaved trees that lose their leaves in winter).
notes.tip: Early settlement and forest clearance is a strong aspect to choose when asked to discuss how biomes are altered by human activity.

notes.h: Early settlement: first clearance by farmers (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The first big change came when people stopped hunting and gathering and began to farm. Farming needs open land, so forest had to go.
points: Mesolithic hunter-gatherers (the Middle Stone Age, people who lived by hunting and gathering) had little impact on the forest.

Farming (the Neolithic, the New Stone Age) reached Ireland about 6,000 years ago, about 4000 BC. Farmers cleared forest with stone axes and fire to grow cereals and graze animals. This was the start of human alteration of the Irish biome.

A sharp fall in elm pollen (found in layers of old soil and bog) around this time, the elm decline, is seen across Ireland and Britain. Clearance by farmers and elm disease are both thought to have contributed.
notes.tip: The elm decline has more than one cause. Do not say farmers alone caused it.

notes.h: Céide Fields, north Co. Mayo (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The Céide Fields show what clearance did to Irish soils. Farmland created by clearance was later buried by bog.
points: Neolithic farmers built stone-walled fields here, about 5,500 years ago. The fields are among the oldest known field systems in the world.

Blanket bog (a thick peat cover over wide areas of upland and west-coast land) later covered the fields. Forest clearance, a wetter climate and leaching (nutrients washed out of the soil by rain) turned the forest soils into bog, and peat grew over the walls.
A local teacher, Patrick Caulfield, found the stone walls under the bog while cutting turf in the 1930s. His son, the archaeologist Séamas Caulfield, later studied the site.
notes.tip: Céide Fields are in north Co. Mayo, not Co. Sligo. Use the site to show clearance followed by soil leaching and peat growth.

notes.h: Early settlement: clearance in the 16th and 17th centuries (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Clearance went on for thousands of years, but the greatest loss of Irish forest came much later, under conquest and trade.
points: Earlier clearance continued through the Bronze and Iron Ages and in early Christian and medieval farming.
The great clearance came in the 16th and 17th centuries, during the Tudor conquest and plantations. Woods were felled for timber exports, shipbuilding, barrel staves and charcoal for ironworks.
Woods were also felled to remove cover used by Irish resistance, because forest gave fighters places to hide.
By 1900 Ireland was among the least wooded countries in Europe, with about 1% of the island forested.
Forest cover is now about 11%, mostly conifer plantations (cone-bearing evergreen trees grown in rows), so most new forest is not the original woodland.
notes.tip: For the 16th and 17th century clearance, give the uses of the timber and the military reason.

notes.h: Early settlement: results for the Irish biome (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Clearance did not just remove trees. It changed the land cover, the wildlife and the soils.
points: Native deciduous forest was replaced by farmland, hedgerows, bog and grassland, which is why little of the original forest remains.
Woodland species declined because their habitat was lost. The wolf was hunted to extinction, the last one generally said to have been killed in the late 1700s.

Soils under heath (open land of low shrubs such as heather) were leached and podzolised (made acidic and infertile, with a pale layer where nutrients have washed out), and blanket bog spread across the uplands.
notes.tip: Give results for vegetation, animals and soils, with the wolf as the named animal example.

notes.h: Early settlement: modern response in Ireland (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Ireland has tried to bring trees back, but the new forests are not the old ones.
points: State afforestation (planting trees on land that had none) has mostly used fast-growing, non-native conifers, chiefly Sitka spruce (native to western North America), because they grow quickly for timber.
Sitka plantations form a new, species-poor habitat, with few kinds of plant and animal, and acidify soils and water.
Native woodland survives in remnants, such as the oakwoods of Killarney National Park, Co. Kerry, and the Reenadinna yew wood on the Muckross peninsula, a rare pure yew wood.
notes.tip: When describing the modern response, give both the plantations and their downsides, and name Killarney for the native remnants.

notes.h: Early settlement: the Mediterranean and a global example (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Forests around the Mediterranean Sea have been cut since ancient times, so the damage there is a clear European example.
points: Deforestation since ancient times, for shipbuilding, fuel, farming and goat grazing, degraded the evergreen oak and pine forest to maquis (dense scrub) and garrigue (low, open scrub on thin soils).
Soil erosion on the cleared slopes followed, because tree roots no longer held the soil. There is more on this in A Peripheral European Region: the Mezzogiorno.
The cedars of Lebanon, prized by the ancient Egyptians and Phoenicians for shipbuilding and temples, survive only in small groves, such as the Cedars of God grove, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Global example, Iceland: birch woodland was cleared and grazed after settlement. There is more on this in Human interference with soils.
notes.tip: Use the Mediterranean as the European example of early clearance. Name maquis and garrigue and the cedars of Lebanon.

notes.h: Felling of tropical rainforests: scale of Amazon clearance (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The Amazon in Brazil is the main case study for felling (cutting down) tropical rainforest. Satellites measure how fast it is being cleared, and the rate has risen and fallen sharply.
points: Brazil's space agency, INPE, measures annual deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon by satellite (the PRODES programme).
Clearance peaked at about 27,800 km² in 2004, fell to about 4,600 km² in 2012, rose to about 13,000 km² in 2021, and fell again from 2023 under renewed enforcement.
Close to a fifth of the original Amazon forest has been cleared, so a large share of the biome is already gone.
notes.tip: Use only the rounded figures for these dates. Describe the 2019 to 2022 rise and the 2023 fall as weaker or renewed enforcement, without naming politicians. Do not give daily or per-minute deforestation rates.

notes.h: Felling of tropical rainforests: farming and logging causes in the Amazon (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Forest is cleared to make money from the land. Farming and timber are the first group of causes, and cattle ranching is the biggest.
points: Cattle ranching is the largest single cause and accounts for most of the cleared land in the Brazilian Amazon. It is the cause, not soya or logging, to name first.
Soya farming, for example, spread north from Mato Grosso. Much of the soya is exported as animal feed, including to Europe and China, which links the forest to distant demand.
Logging of hardwoods: selective logging (taking only chosen valuable trees) opens roads and gaps in the canopy that lead to further clearance.
Government policy and debt, together with global demand for beef, soya, timber and minerals, drive clearance.
notes.tip: Cattle ranching, not soya or logging, is the largest single cause of Amazon clearance. Give each cause as its own point with a named example.

notes.h: Felling of tropical rainforests: roads, mining and dams in the Amazon (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Big building projects open the forest up. Roads bring settlers, mines need power and fuel, and dams flood land.
points: Road building and planned settlement: the Trans-Amazonian Highway (BR-230), begun in the early 1970s by the military government, opened the Amazon to settlers from the poor, drought-prone north-east.
BR-364 into Rondônia, paved in the 1980s with World Bank support (the Polonoroeste programme), led to a fishbone pattern of clearings along its side roads, which shows up on satellite images.
Mining: Carajás, Pará state, is one of the world's largest iron-ore mines, operated by Vale and opened in the 1980s. A railway carries the ore to the coast.
Charcoal-fuelled pig-iron smelters (furnaces making crude iron) near Carajás used forest wood, so mining cleared forest beyond the mine itself.
Illegal gold mining (garimpo) on Yanomami land pollutes rivers with mercury.

Hydroelectric dams: the Belo Monte dam on the Xingu River, Pará, completed in 2019, is one of the world's largest hydroelectric schemes by capacity. It flooded forest and land, diverted the river past the Volta Grande (Big Bend), and displaced thousands of people.
The Kayapó and other indigenous groups strongly opposed Belo Monte. There is more on river impacts in Human interaction: river processes.
notes.tip: Give each cause its own point with a named example: the Trans-Amazonian Highway, BR-364, Carajás, garimpo and Belo Monte. Here Belo Monte is a forest and people example.

notes.h: Felling of tropical rainforests: impacts on the Amazon biome (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Removing the trees affects the animals, the soil, the water cycle and the climate. The effects feed into each other.
points: Loss of habitat and species, many of them endemic to the region (found nowhere else), so animals that depend on the forest lose their homes.
Fragmentation of the remaining forest (breaking it into patches) creates edge effects, as the forest edge is drier, hotter and more exposed.
The nutrient cycle is broken: cleared latosols (the deep, nutrient-poor red tropical soils) lose their fertility within a few years, and pasture is abandoned.
Soil erosion and a hard laterite crust (an iron-rich layer that bakes hard) form on the exposed land, and rivers silt up.
Less evapotranspiration (water given off by plants into the air) means less rainfall downwind and longer dry seasons, and fires become more frequent.
The forest stores huge amounts of carbon; burning and decay release it to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide.

Scientists, notably Carlos Nobre and Thomas Lovejoy, have warned that losing about 20 to 25% of the forest could push parts of the Amazon past a tipping point (a threshold after which change cannot easily be reversed) towards degraded savanna.
notes.tip: Describe the Amazon as a major carbon store and source of rainfall. Do not say it produces 20% of the world's oxygen. Cover vegetation, animals, soils and climate.

notes.h: Felling of tropical rainforests: impacts on people (Higher Level only)
notes.b: People live in the rainforest, and clearance harms indigenous peoples (the original inhabitants) through loss of land, disease and conflict.
points: Indigenous peoples lose their land, suffer disease, and face violence and conflict with ranchers and miners, for example the Yanomami and the gold miners.
Chico Mendes, a rubber tapper and union leader who campaigned to protect the forest, was murdered by a rancher's family at Xapuri, Acre, on 22 December 1988.
In 2023 the Brazilian government declared a public health emergency in Yanomami territory after illegal gold mining caused malnutrition and disease.
notes.tip: Name the Yanomami and Chico Mendes as the examples of impacts on indigenous peoples.

notes.h: Felling of tropical rainforests: responses and evaluation (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Brazil has laws, markets and monitoring to slow clearance. How well they work has changed with national policy.
points: Brazil's Forest Code requires landowners in the Amazon to keep 80% of their land as forest, the legal reserve. The code was revised in 2012.
The Amazon Soy Moratorium (2006): major traders agreed not to buy soya grown on newly deforested Amazon land, which removes the market for that soya.
The Amazon Fund (2008), with Norway the largest donor, pays for forest protection, so money from abroad supports enforcement.
INPE's PRODES annual figures and DETER near-real-time alerts guide enforcement by IBAMA, the federal environment agency, so illegal clearing can be found and acted on.

Protected areas, indigenous territories and extractive reserves, where local people harvest rubber and nuts sustainably, were set up after Chico Mendes's death; the Chico Mendes Extractive Reserve in Acre is one example.
Evaluation: the falls and rises in clearance show that protection depends on political will and enforcement.
notes.tip: Evaluate by linking the fall to 2012, the rise to 2021 and the fall again from 2023 to changes in policy and enforcement. Success depends on political will and enforcement.

notes.h: Felling of tropical rainforests: South-East Asia (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Rainforest in Borneo and Sumatra is a second example. Here the main driver is palm oil, a vegetable oil from oil palm trees.
points: Indonesia and Malaysia together produce about 85% of the world's palm oil, so these two countries dominate world supply.
Lowland rainforest and peat swamp forest (waterlogged forest growing on thick peat) in Borneo and Sumatra are cleared for oil palm plantations and timber.
Drained and burned peat causes regional haze (smoke pollution), notably in 1997 and 2015, affecting Singapore and Malaysia.
The Bornean orangutan was listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN in 2016, making it the flagship threatened species (the animal that stands for the wider loss) of this clearance.
notes.tip: Use palm oil and logging in Indonesia and Malaysia, peat swamp haze and the orangutan as your second example.

notes.h: Felling of tropical rainforests: the European link (Higher Level only)
notes.b: European consumers drive some of the clearance, and the EU has begun to act on it.
points: Europe's demand for beef, soya (as animal feed), timber and palm oil drives felling.

The EU Deforestation Regulation (adopted 2023) will require firms selling beef, soya, palm oil, cocoa, coffee, rubber and timber in the EU to prove they were not grown on land deforested after 2020. Its application has been delayed.

notes.h: Intensive agriculture: what it is (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Intensive farming tries to get as much food as possible from each patch of land. This changes the habitats on and around the farm.
points: Intensive farming uses high inputs of capital (money), machinery, fertiliser, pesticides and water to get maximum output per hectare.
It creates monocultures (one crop grown over a large area), larger fields and drained wetlands, so habitats become fewer and simpler.

notes.h: Intensive agriculture: dairying and tillage in Ireland, the changes (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Irish farming has intensified in both dairying (milk production) and tillage (growing crops on ploughed land). The changes removed habitats and polluted water.
points: EU milk quotas (limits on how much milk each farm could produce) ended on 1 April 2015, after which Irish dairy herds expanded.
Hedgerows were removed and fields enlarged; wetlands and callows (wet meadows beside a river) were drained; species-rich meadows were reseeded with ryegrass, a single grass grown for feed.
Silage (grass cut and stored for animal feed) replaced hay. Earlier, mechanised cutting destroys the nests of ground-nesting birds such as the corncrake.
The corncrake has declined to a small population mainly in north-west Donegal, west Mayo and the Shannon Callows.
Wild bees and farmland birds have declined, because the hedgerows and meadows that fed and sheltered them were lost.
notes.tip: Give the changes to the land, then the effect on wildlife, with the corncrake as the named bird.

notes.h: Intensive agriculture: dairying and tillage in Ireland, pollution and responses (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Heavy use of fertiliser and slurry (liquid animal manure) affects water and the atmosphere. Policies now try to reduce it and help wildlife.
points: Heavy use of fertiliser and slurry raises nitrate levels in rivers and estuaries, especially in the south and south-east.
The extra nutrients cause eutrophication of lakes (an overgrowth of algae that uses up the oxygen in the water).
Agriculture is the largest source of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions, over a third of the total, according to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

Responses: the Nitrates Directive (1991); agri-environment schemes (payments to farmers for farming that helps nature) REPS (1994), GLAS (2015) and ACRES (2023); and the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan, begun in 2015.
notes.tip: Include a response with your Irish example: the Nitrates Directive, the agri-environment schemes or the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan.

notes.h: Intensive agriculture: a European example (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The EU's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP, the EU's system of farm payments) shows how policy can drive intensification across a continent.
points: The Common Agricultural Policy began in 1962. Guaranteed prices encouraged farmers to remove hedgerows, enlarge fields and drain wetlands, notably in the arable east of England (East Anglia).
Food surpluses, the butter mountains and wine lakes, followed in the 1980s, because guaranteed prices encouraged farmers to produce more than was needed.
Later reforms, from 1992 onwards, began paying farmers for environmental farming.

notes.h: Intensive agriculture: temperate grassland and the rainforest link (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Intensive farming has also replaced grassland biomes, and it overlaps with rainforest clearance.
points: The tallgrass prairie of North America (temperate grassland) has been almost entirely converted to farmland; only a few per cent survives.
The Dust Bowl, when ploughed grassland soils blew away, is an example of the soil loss that followed. There is more on this in Human interference with soils.
Cattle and soya in the Amazon are also intensive agriculture; the impacts are those listed under the felling of tropical rainforests.

notes.h: Intensive agriculture: irrigation and the Aral Sea (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Irrigation (supplying water to crops by channels) can destroy a whole lake. The Aral Sea in Central Asia is the case study.
points: The Aral Sea lies on the border of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. In 1960 it was the world's fourth-largest lake.
From the 1960s Soviet planners diverted its feeder rivers, the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, to irrigate cotton and rice in the desert, so less water reached the sea.
The sea shrank to a fraction of its former size and split into separate parts. Its salinity rose and the fishing industry collapsed.
Former fishing ports such as Moynaq (Muynak), Uzbekistan, were left far from the shore, with ships stranded on the dry seabed.
Dust storms carry salt and pesticide residues from the exposed seabed onto farmland and people, with health effects.
Salinisation (build-up of salt in the soil) and waterlogging damaged the irrigated soils.
The Kok-Aral Dam (2005), built by Kazakhstan with World Bank funding, raised the level of the small North Aral Sea, and fishing has partly recovered there.
notes.tip: The Aral Sea shrank because of irrigation, not climate change. It is one of the world's worst environmental disasters.

notes.h: Industrial development: acid rain in Europe (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Factories and power stations release gases that make rain acidic. The pollution travels, so it damages forests and lakes far from its source.
points: Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from coal- and oil-burning power stations, industry and vehicles form acids that are carried downwind, often across national borders.

Acid rain acidified thousands of lakes in southern Norway and Sweden from the 1960s to the 1980s; fish died out in many of them. Its source was largely the emissions of other countries, so the countries that suffered were not the ones that caused it.
Effects on coniferous forests include needle loss, dieback (trees dying from the top down) and nutrient leaching from the soil.
Effects on lakes include fish being killed and aluminium being released into the water.

The Black Triangle, where the borders of Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic meet, had lignite-burning power stations, so large amounts of acid gases were released (lignite is a low-grade, dirty brown coal).
Large areas of spruce forest in the Ore Mountains (Erzgebirge) and neighbouring ranges died in the 1970s and 1980s, a process known as Waldsterben (forest death).
notes.tip: Acid rain in Scandinavia came largely from other countries' emissions, so it is a transboundary problem.

notes.h: Industrial development: responses to acid rain and Moneypoint (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Because acid rain crosses borders, countries had to act together. The same fixes were applied at home.
points: Responses: the Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution (1979); EU limits on power-station emissions; flue-gas desulphurisation (removing sulphur from chimney gases); and liming of lakes in Sweden and Norway, which neutralises their acidity.
Sulphur dioxide emissions in Europe have since fallen by well over half, and many forests and lakes have partly recovered.
Moneypoint, Co. Clare, on the Shannon Estuary, was Ireland's only coal-fired power station, opened in the 1980s.
Flue-gas desulphurisation was later fitted to cut its sulphur emissions, so less acid rain formed. ESB ended coal-burning there in 2025.

notes.h: Industrial development: Bord na Móna and Irish peatlands (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Industry changed the raised bogs of the Midlands. A raised bog is a dome of peat that formed over thousands of years, and it was harvested for fuel.
points: Bord na Móna, a state company set up in 1946, harvested milled peat on a large scale from the Midland raised bogs for power stations and briquettes (peat fuel blocks).
The peat-burning power stations at Shannonbridge (West Offaly) and Lanesborough (Lough Ree) closed in December 2020. Bord na Móna ended peat harvesting in 2021, under its Brown to Green plan.

Its cutaway bogs (bogs where the peat has been removed) are being rehabilitated and rewetted. Lough Boora Discovery Park, Co. Offaly, is cutaway bog converted to wetlands, woodland and amenity land, so land damaged by harvesting gains new habitats.
Clara Bog, Co. Offaly, is one of the largest relatively intact raised bogs in Ireland, and is a nature reserve and Special Area of Conservation, so it shows what an undamaged raised bog looks like.
Peatlands cover about a fifth of Ireland, so changes to them alter a large share of the country's land.
notes.tip: Name the Midland peat stations if you are unsure of their counties. Use Clara Bog as the protected intact bog.

notes.h: Industrial development: oil sands in Canada (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Getting oil out of sand needs huge areas to be dug up, so the boreal forest above is destroyed.
points: The Athabasca oil sands, around Fort McMurray in northern Alberta, Canada, are mined by surface (open-pit) methods that strip away boreal forest (northern coniferous forest) and muskeg (peatland) to reach bitumen-soaked sand.
The mining produces large tailings ponds (ponds of polluted waste water) and high greenhouse gas emissions per barrel.
Companies must reclaim mined land (restore it), but little of it has been certified as reclaimed.
notes.tip: Use the oil sands as an example of mining that removes boreal forest and peatland, and name the tailings ponds.

notes.h: Industrial development: oil pollution in the Niger Delta (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Oil extraction can pollute a whole delta, where creeks, mangroves and farms are close together.
points: Oil has been produced in the Niger Delta, Nigeria, since the late 1950s, by Shell and others.
Repeated spills from pipelines, and theft, have polluted creeks, mangrove forest (coastal forest growing in salt water) and farmland.
A UNEP study of Ogoniland (2011) found pollution so widespread that a clean-up could take 25 to 30 years.
notes.tip: Name mangroves and farmland as the biomes and land affected by the Niger Delta spills.

notes.h: Industrial development: Chernobyl (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A nuclear accident killed a forest, and then the absence of people let wildlife return.
points: The Chernobyl nuclear power station in Ukraine, then part of the USSR, exploded on 26 April 1986.
Radiation killed a nearby pine forest, because the trees absorbed it, whose needles turned reddish-brown, the Red Forest.
A 30 km exclusion zone was evacuated. With people gone, so that wildlife is undisturbed, wildlife such as wolves, elk, wild boar and the reintroduced Przewalski's horse has become common there.
notes.tip: Use Chernobyl for the Red Forest and for the exclusion zone as a refuge for wildlife.

notes.h: Industrial development: wider effects (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Industry affects biomes beyond the factory site, through the atmosphere and through the spread of towns and factories.
points: Greenhouse gases from industry shift climate belts and stress biomes, through coral bleaching, thawing tundra permafrost (ground that stays frozen all year), and more drought and fire. There is more on global warming in Option: Global Interdependence.
Urban and industrial sprawl (the spread of towns and factories over open land) replaces habitats and seals the soil beneath.

notes.h: Evaluation: is human alteration always negative? (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Human activity can also repair biomes, so a balanced answer weighs benefits against losses.
points: Not all alteration is negative. Protected areas, rewilding, rewetting of bogs, results-based farming (farmers paid for the wildlife results they achieve, as in the Burren) and pollution controls can restore biomes.
The central evaluation is the balance between economic gain and the loss of biomes.
notes.tip: When asked to discuss how biomes are altered by human activity, use any four aspects from the four activities, with case studies.

keyTerms.definition: The vegetation that would grow in an area if it were left undisturbed by humans.
The New Stone Age, when farming first reached Ireland about 6,000 years ago.
A peat bog that spreads across gently sloping or upland ground, often over former forest or farmland.
Planting trees on land that has not recently been wooded.
Dense Mediterranean scrub that replaces evergreen oak and pine forest after clearance.
Low, open Mediterranean scrub growing on thin soils.
The growing of a single crop over a large area.
The enrichment of water by nutrients from fertiliser and slurry, which can cause algal growth and oxygen loss.
Rain made acidic by sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning fuels.
A process that removes sulphur dioxide from the smoke of power stations.
A pond holding the waste water and sediment left after mining.
The change in conditions and species at the edge of a fragmented patch of forest.
The threshold beyond which a system changes irreversibly to a different state.
A protected area where local people harvest forest products such as rubber and nuts sustainably.

factCards.term: Neolithic farmers: how they began altering Ireland's forest
factCards.definition: By about 6,000 years ago forest covered almost all of Ireland. Farming arrived then (about 4000 BC), clearing forest with stone axes and fire for crops and grazing. The elm decline in pollen dates from this time (farmers and elm disease both played a part).

factCards.term: Céide Fields: what they show and how they were found
factCards.definition: North Co. Mayo: stone-walled Neolithic fields about 5,500 years old, among the oldest known field systems, later buried as clearance, a wetter climate and leaching turned forest soil to blanket bog. Patrick Caulfield found the walls cutting turf in the 1930s.

factCards.term: Ireland's great forest clearance: when, why and the result
factCards.definition: In the 16th and 17th centuries (Tudor conquest and plantations), woods were felled for timber exports, shipbuilding, barrel staves and charcoal for ironworks, and to remove cover for Irish resistance. About 1% of Ireland was forested by 1900; now about 11%.

factCards.term: Forest clearance in Ireland: three results for the biome
factCards.definition: Native deciduous forest was replaced by farmland, hedgerows, bog and grassland; woodland species declined, and the wolf was hunted to extinction (the last in the late 1700s); soils under heath were leached and podzolised, and blanket bog spread on the uplands.

factCards.term: Irish forests today: conifer plantations and native remnants
factCards.definition: State afforestation mostly uses Sitka spruce, native to western North America, giving species-poor plantations that acidify soils and water. Native remnants include the oakwoods of Killarney National Park and the Reenadinna yew wood on the Muckross peninsula.

factCards.term: Mediterranean forest clearance: causes and results
factCards.definition: Since ancient times, felling for shipbuilding, fuel and farming, plus goat grazing, degraded evergreen oak and pine forest to maquis and garrigue, with soil erosion. The cedars of Lebanon survive only in small groves such as the Cedars of God (UNESCO).

factCards.term: Amazon deforestation: INPE's figures and their trend
factCards.definition: Measured by satellite (PRODES): a peak of about 27,800 km² in 2004; a fall to about 4,600 km² in 2012; a rise to about 13,000 km² in 2021; a fall again from 2023 under renewed enforcement. Close to a fifth of the original forest has been cleared.

factCards.term: Amazon clearance: cattle, soya and logging
factCards.definition: Cattle ranching is the largest single cause, accounting for most cleared land; soya spread north from Mato Grosso, much of it exported as animal feed to Europe and China; selective logging of hardwoods opens roads and canopy gaps that lead to more clearance.

factCards.term: Amazon roads: two named roads and their effects
factCards.definition: The Trans-Amazonian Highway (BR-230), begun in the early 1970s by the military government, brought settlers from the drought-prone north-east. BR-364 into Rondônia, paved in the 1980s with World Bank support, left a fishbone pattern of clearings.

factCards.term: Amazon mining and dams: three named examples
factCards.definition: Carajás, Pará: a huge iron-ore mine (Vale, 1980s) whose pig-iron smelters burned forest charcoal; illegal gold mining (garimpo) on Yanomami land pollutes rivers with mercury; the Belo Monte dam on the Xingu (2019) flooded forest and displaced thousands.

factCards.term: Rainforest felling: impacts on plants, animals and soils
factCards.definition: Loss of habitat and many endemic species; fragmentation, with drier, hotter edge effects; the nutrient cycle breaks, so cleared latosols lose fertility within a few years and pasture is abandoned; soil erosion and laterite crust; rivers silt up.

factCards.term: Amazon felling: effects on climate and the tipping point
factCards.definition: Less evapotranspiration means less rain downwind, longer dry seasons and more fires; burning and decay release stored carbon as carbon dioxide. Carlos Nobre and Thomas Lovejoy warn that losing about 20–25% could tip parts of the forest to degraded savanna.

factCards.term: Amazon felling: impacts on indigenous and forest peoples
factCards.definition: Loss of land, disease, and violence from ranchers and miners. Chico Mendes, a rubber tapper and union leader, was murdered at Xapuri, Acre, on 22 December 1988; in 2023 Brazil declared a health emergency in Yanomami territory after illegal gold mining.

factCards.term: Amazon protection: five responses and the lesson they teach
factCards.definition: The Forest Code (keep 80% of land as forest; revised 2012); the Soy Moratorium (2006); the Amazon Fund (2008; Norway the largest donor); INPE satellite alerts guiding IBAMA; extractive reserves. Changing clearance rates show success depends on enforcement.

factCards.term: South-East Asia: palm oil and its impacts on the rainforest
factCards.definition: Indonesia and Malaysia produce about 85% of the world's palm oil. Rainforest and peat swamp in Borneo and Sumatra are cleared; burning drained peat caused haze in 1997 and 2015 over Singapore and Malaysia; the Bornean orangutan is Critically Endangered (2016).

factCards.term: Europe's link to rainforest felling
factCards.definition: European demand for beef, soya as animal feed, timber and palm oil drives felling. The EU Deforestation Regulation (adopted 2023) will make firms prove such products were not grown on land deforested after 2020; its application has been delayed.

factCards.term: Intensive dairying and tillage in Ireland: impacts on the biome
factCards.definition: After milk quotas ended (1 April 2015) herds grew; hedgerows were removed, wetlands and callows drained, meadows reseeded with ryegrass; slurry and fertiliser raise river nitrates; silage cutting destroys corncrake nests; bees and farmland birds decline.

factCards.term: Common Agricultural Policy: how it intensified farming
factCards.definition: Begun in 1962, its guaranteed prices encouraged hedgerow removal, larger fields and wetland drainage, notably in East Anglia; food surpluses (butter mountains, wine lakes) followed in the 1980s; reforms from 1992 began paying for environmental farming.

factCards.term: Aral Sea: why it shrank
factCards.definition: On the Kazakhstan–Uzbekistan border; the world's fourth-largest lake in 1960. From the 1960s Soviet planners diverted its feeder rivers, the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, to irrigate cotton and rice, so it shrank and split: irrigation, not climate change.

factCards.term: Aral Sea: effects and a partial recovery
factCards.definition: Salinity rose and fishing collapsed, leaving Moynaq far from shore with ships stranded; dust storms carry salt and pesticides onto farms and people; irrigated soils were salinised. The Kok-Aral Dam (2005) raised the North Aral Sea; fishing partly revived.

factCards.term: Acid rain in Scandinavia: cause and effects on lakes
factCards.definition: Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from British and Central European industry were carried across borders; from the 1960s to the 1980s thousands of lakes in southern Norway and Sweden were acidified, aluminium was released and fish died out in many.

factCards.term: Black Triangle: where it is and what happened to its forests
factCards.definition: Where Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic meet, lignite-burning power stations caused acid rain; large areas of spruce forest in the Ore Mountains (Erzgebirge) died in the 1970s and 1980s (Waldsterben), with needle loss, dieback and soil leaching.

factCards.term: Acid rain in Europe: responses and results
factCards.definition: The Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution (1979); EU power-station emission limits; flue-gas desulphurisation; liming of lakes in Sweden and Norway. Sulphur dioxide emissions fell by well over half; many forests and lakes partly recovered.

factCards.term: Bord na Móna: its industrial peat harvesting and how it ended
factCards.definition: A state company set up in 1946, it harvested milled peat on a large scale for power stations and briquettes. The Shannonbridge and Lanesborough peat stations closed in December 2020, and peat harvesting ended in 2021 under its Brown to Green plan.

factCards.term: Irish bogs after industrial peat cutting: two named sites
factCards.definition: Cutaway bogs are being rehabilitated and rewetted: Lough Boora Discovery Park, Co. Offaly, is cutaway bog turned into wetland, woodland and amenity land. Clara Bog, Co. Offaly, is one of the largest relatively intact raised bogs, now a nature reserve.

factCards.term: Athabasca oil sands: impacts on the boreal biome
factCards.definition: Around Fort McMurray, northern Alberta, Canada, open-pit mining strips away boreal forest and muskeg (peatland) to reach bitumen-soaked sand, leaving large tailings ponds and high emissions per barrel; little mined land has been certified as reclaimed.

factCards.term: Niger Delta: how oil has damaged the biome
factCards.definition: Oil has been produced since the late 1950s (Shell and others); pipeline spills and theft polluted creeks, mangroves and farmland. A 2011 UNEP study of Ogoniland said a clean-up could take 25 to 30 years. Campaigner Ken Saro-Wiwa was executed in 1995.

factCards.term: Chernobyl: how the 1986 accident altered the biome
factCards.definition: The nuclear plant in Ukraine (then the USSR) exploded on 26 April 1986; radiation killed a pine forest, the Red Forest. A 30 km exclusion zone was evacuated; without people, wolves, elk, wild boar and reintroduced Przewalski's horses have become common.

questions.prompt: Examine how each of the following alters biomes: the felling of tropical rainforests; intensive agricultural practices; industrial development.
questions.model: Three aspects of roughly equal weight. The felling of tropical rainforests: the Amazon, with its causes (cattle ranching as the largest cause, soya, logging, roads such as the Trans-Amazonian Highway and BR-364, mining at Carajás, and the Belo Monte dam), its impacts (habitat and species loss, a broken nutrient cycle, altered rainfall, carbon release and a tipping point) and responses (the Forest Code, the Soy Moratorium, the Amazon Fund and enforcement). Intensive agriculture: in Ireland, with hedgerow loss, drainage, silage cutting and the corncrake, eutrophication and the CAP, and the Aral Sea as an irrigation case. Industrial development: acid rain in Scandinavia and the Black Triangle with forest death, and Bord na Móna's peat extraction in the Midlands with rehabilitation. Each aspect should name its case studies, impacts on vegetation, animals, soils and climate, and a response.

questions.prompt: Biomes have been altered by human activities. Discuss.
questions.model: Four aspects, with one case study for each. Early settlement and forest clearance: Irish post-glacial forest cleared by Neolithic farmers, shown at the Céide Fields, followed by the 16th and 17th century clearance and the later conifer afforestation with its native woodland remnants. Felling of tropical rainforests: the Amazon, with causes, impacts and responses. Intensive agriculture: Irish dairying and tillage, or the Aral Sea. Industrial development: acid rain in Europe or peat extraction at Bord na Móna. Balance the discussion with a note that protection and restoration can reverse some alteration.

questions.prompt: Examine the impact of early settlement and forest clearance on one biome you have studied.
questions.model: The temperate deciduous forest of Ireland only. Post-glacial forest of birch, hazel, pine, oak, elm and ash covered almost all of the island by about 6,000 years ago. Neolithic farmers cleared it with stone axes and fire, and the elm decline marks this clearance. The Céide Fields in north Co. Mayo show clearance followed by leaching and blanket bog. The 16th and 17th century clearance for timber, shipbuilding, charcoal and resistance cover left Ireland among the least wooded countries in Europe by 1900. Its impacts include farmland, bog and grassland replacing native forest, the loss of woodland species such as the wolf, and podzolised heath soils. Modern afforestation with Sitka spruce acidifies soils, and native remnants such as the Killarney oakwoods and the Reenadinna yew wood survive.
